title: Der Ranzen, das Hütlein und das Hörnlein
titleEn: The Knapsack, the Hat, and the Horn
part: The Knapsack, the Hat, and the Horn
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 54. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, fieng, hieng, Thür/Thüre, thun, Noth, todt, Armuth, erwiederte und gerieth).
about: KHM 54, a soldier’s tale rather than a nursery one. Three brothers go out to seek their fortune; two stop at a mountain of silver and a mountain of gold, and the third holds out for something better and comes away with a wishing-cloth, which he trades to three charcoal-burners in turn for a knapsack, a hat and a horn — sending conjured soldiers after each of them to take the cloth straight back. There is no moral in it and very little mercy: the hero has his brothers thrashed, breaks a king’s armies, blows down towns and villages, and ends on the throne. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as Armuth, Noth, gieng, thun, funfzig and todt.

sentences.t: Es waren einmal drei Brüder, die waren immer tiefer in Armuth gerathen, und endlich war die Noth so groß, daß sie Hunger leiden mußten und nichts mehr zu beißen und zu brechen hatten.
sentences.l: There were once three brothers, who had fallen ever deeper into poverty, and at last the want was so great that they had to suffer hunger and had nothing more to bite and to break.
sentences.i: There were once three brothers who had sunk deeper and deeper into poverty, until at last their want was so great that they had to go hungry and had nothing left to eat.
sentences.n: “nichts mehr zu beißen und zu brechen” is a set phrase for having nothing whatever to eat — “nothing to bite and to break.” Armuth and Noth keep the archaic th- (modern Armut, Not), and gerathen is modern geraten.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie „es kann so nicht bleiben: es ist besser wir gehen in die Welt und suchen unser Glück.“
sentences.l: Then spoke they “it cannot remain so: it is better we go into the world and seek our fortune.”
sentences.i: Then they said: “It cannot go on like this. Better that we go out into the world and seek our fortune.”
sentences.n: Glück holds both senses at once here — luck and prosperity — and the whole tale turns on it: each brother settles for a different amount of it.

sentences.t: Sie machten sich also auf, und waren schon weite Wege und über viele Grashälmerchen gegangen, aber das Glück war ihnen noch nicht begegnet.
sentences.l: They set themselves out therefore, and had already gone long ways and over many little-blades-of-grass, but fortune had not yet met them.
sentences.i: So they set out, and had already walked long roads and over many a blade of grass, but fortune had not yet come their way.
sentences.n: “über viele Grashälmerchen gegangen” is a homely storyteller’s measure of distance — over many a little blade of grass. Grashälmerchen is a doubled diminutive (Halm, stalk → Hälmchen).

sentences.t: Da gelangten sie eines Tags in einen großen Wald, und mitten darin war ein Berg, und als sie näher kamen, so sahen sie daß der Berg ganz von Silber war.
sentences.l: Then arrived they one day in a great forest, and in the middle of it was a mountain, and when they came nearer, so they saw that the mountain was entirely of silver.
sentences.i: One day they came into a great forest, and in the middle of it stood a mountain; and when they came nearer they saw that the mountain was all of silver.

sentences.t: Da sprach der älteste „nun habe ich das gewünschte Glück gefunden und verlange kein größeres.“
sentences.l: Then spoke the eldest “now have I found the wished-for fortune and demand no greater one.”
sentences.i: Then the eldest said: “Now I have found the fortune I wished for, and ask for no greater.”

sentences.t: Er nahm von dem Silber so viel er nur tragen konnte, kehrte dann um und gieng wieder nach Haus.
sentences.l: He took of the silver as much as he could only carry, turned then about and went home again.
sentences.i: He took as much of the silver as he could possibly carry, then turned back and went home.
sentences.n: “von dem Silber” is partitive — some of the silver — and nur inside the clause means “as much as he possibly could,” not “only.”

sentences.t: Die beiden andern aber sprachen „wir verlangen vom Glück noch etwas mehr als bloßes Silber,“ rührten es nicht an und giengen weiter.
sentences.l: The two others however spoke “we demand of fortune something more than mere silver,” touched it not and went further.
sentences.i: But the other two said: “We ask something more of fortune than mere silver” — and they did not touch it, but walked on.

sentences.t: Nachdem sie abermals ein paar Tage gegangen waren, so kamen sie zu einem Berg, der ganz von Gold war.
sentences.l: After they had gone another couple of days, so came they to a mountain that was entirely of gold.
sentences.i: After they had walked on for another couple of days, they came to a mountain that was all of gold.

sentences.t: Der zweite Bruder stand, besann sich und war ungewiß.
sentences.l: The second brother stood, bethought himself and was uncertain.
sentences.i: The second brother stopped, turned it over in his mind, and could not decide.
sentences.n: stand here is “stood still, halted”; “sich besinnen” is to reflect, to think a thing through.

sentences.t: „Was soll ich thun?“ sprach er, „soll ich mir von dem Golde so viel nehmen, daß ich mein Lebtag genug habe, oder soll ich weiter gehen?“
sentences.l: “What shall I do?” spoke he, “shall I take myself so much of the gold that I have enough my life-day, or shall I go further?”
sentences.i: “What shall I do?” he said. “Shall I take enough of the gold to have plenty all my days, or shall I go on?”
sentences.n: “mein Lebtag” — all my life long, an old fixed accusative of time. thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Endlich faßte er einen Entschluß, füllte in seine Taschen was hinein wollte, sagte seinem Bruder Lebewohl und gieng heim.
sentences.l: At last seized he a resolve, filled into his pockets what wanted in, said his brother farewell and went home.
sentences.i: At last he made up his mind, stuffed into his pockets whatever would go in, bade his brother farewell and went home.
sentences.n: “was hinein wollte” — “what wanted in,” i.e. as much as would fit; German lets wollen stand alone with the verb of motion understood.

sentences.t: Der dritte aber sprach „Silber und Gold das rührt mich nicht: ich will meinem Glück nicht absagen, vielleicht ist mir etwas besseres beschert.“
sentences.l: The third however spoke “silver and gold, that moves me not: I will not renounce my fortune, perhaps something better is allotted to me.”
sentences.i: But the third said: “Silver and gold — those do not move me. I will not give up on my fortune; perhaps something better is in store for me.”
sentences.n: beschert (from bescheren) is what fate or a giver allots you — the same verb used of Christmas presents.

sentences.t: Er zog weiter, und als er drei Tage gegangen war, so kam er in einen Wald, der noch größer war als die vorigen und gar kein Ende nehmen wollte; und da er nichts zu essen und zu trinken fand, so war er nahe daran zu verschmachten.
sentences.l: He drew further, and when he had gone three days, so came he into a forest that was still greater than the previous ones and would take no end at all; and since he found nothing to eat and to drink, so was he near to languishing away.
sentences.i: He journeyed on; and when he had walked three days he came into a forest greater than the ones before, one that would take no end at all. And since he found nothing to eat or drink, he was near to perishing.
sentences.n: “kein Ende nehmen wollte” — “would take no end”: wollen here is not a wish but a tendency, as English “the road would not end.” verschmachten is to pine away for want of food and drink.

sentences.t: Da stieg er auf einen hohen Baum, ob er da oben Waldes Ende sehen möchte, aber so weit sein Auge reichte sah er nichts als die Gipfel der Bäume.
sentences.l: Then climbed he up a high tree, whether he might up there see the forest’s end, but as far as his eye reached he saw nothing but the tops of the trees.
sentences.i: So he climbed a tall tree, to see whether from up there he might make out the end of the forest; but as far as his eye reached he saw nothing but treetops.
sentences.n: ob introduces what he climbs up to find out — “(to see) whether”; möchte is subjunctive, keeping it a hope. “Waldes Ende” sets the genitive before its noun, an elevated old order.

sentences.t: Da begab er sich von dem Baume wieder herunter zu steigen, aber der Hunger quälte ihn, und er dachte „wenn ich nur noch einmal meinen Leib ersättigen könnte.“
sentences.l: Then set he himself to climbing down from the tree again, but the hunger tormented him, and he thought “if I could only once more sate my body.”
sentences.i: Then he set about climbing down from the tree again; but hunger tormented him, and he thought: “If only I could fill my belly once more.”
sentences.n: “sich begeben zu” here is to set about doing a thing; elsewhere sich begeben means to betake oneself somewhere. Leib is the body as the seat of appetite — his belly.

sentences.t: Als er herab kam, sah er mit Erstaunen unter dem Baum einen Tisch, der mit Speisen reichlich besetzt war, die ihm entgegen dampften.
sentences.l: When he came down, saw he with astonishment under the tree a table that was richly set with dishes, which steamed toward him.
sentences.i: When he came down he saw, to his astonishment, a table beneath the tree richly laid with dishes whose steam rose to meet him.
sentences.n: entgegendampfen — “to steam toward”; German builds such verbs freely out of entgegen (toward, to meet).

sentences.t: „Diesmal,“ sprach er, „ist mein Wunsch zu rechter Zeit erfüllt worden,“ und ohne zu fragen wer das Essen gebracht und wer es gekocht hätte, nahte er sich dem Tisch und aß mit Lust bis er seinen Hunger gestillt hatte.
sentences.l: “This time,” spoke he, “has my wish been fulfilled at the right time,” and without asking who had brought the food and who had cooked it, he neared himself to the table and ate with relish until he had stilled his hunger.
sentences.i: “This time,” he said, “my wish has been granted at the right moment” — and without asking who had brought the food or who had cooked it, he drew near the table and ate with relish until his hunger was stilled.
sentences.n: “sich nahen” (+ dative) is an elevated word for approaching. gebracht… gekocht hätte is subjunctive: the questions he does not put.

sentences.t: Als er fertig war, dachte er „es wäre doch Schade wenn das feine Tischtüchlein hier in dem Walde verderben sollte,“ legte es säuberlich zusammen und steckte es ein.
sentences.l: When he was finished, thought he “it would be a pity though if the fine little-tablecloth should spoil here in the forest,” folded it neatly together and pocketed it.
sentences.i: When he had finished he thought: “It would be a pity if this fine little cloth should go to ruin here in the forest” — and he folded it up neatly and put it in his pocket.
sentences.n: einstecken is to pocket a thing. Tischtüchlein is a little Tischtuch (tablecloth); the diminutive stays with the cloth for the rest of the tale.

sentences.t: Darauf gieng er weiter, und Abends, als der Hunger sich wieder regte, wollte er sein Tüchlein auf die Probe stellen, breitete es aus und sagte „so wünsche ich daß du abermals mit guten Speisen besetzt wärest,“ und kaum war der Wunsch über seine Lippen gekommen, so standen so viel Schüsseln mit dem schönsten Essen darauf, als nur Platz hatten.
sentences.l: Thereupon went he further, and in the evening, when the hunger stirred itself again, he wanted to put his little-cloth to the test, spread it out and said “so I wish that you were set with good dishes again,” and scarcely had the wish come over his lips, so there stood upon it as many bowls with the finest food as only had room.
sentences.i: Then he walked on; and in the evening, when hunger stirred again, he thought to put his little cloth to the test: he spread it out and said, “Now I wish you were laid with good food again” — and scarcely had the wish crossed his lips when there stood upon it as many dishes of the finest fare as could find room.
sentences.n: “auf die Probe stellen” = to put to the test. wärest is subjunctive inside the wish. “als nur Platz hatten” — “as only had room,” i.e. as many as would fit.

sentences.t: „Jetzt merke ich,“ sagte er, „in welcher Küche für mich gekocht wird; du sollst mir lieber sein als der Berg von Silber und Gold,“ denn er sah wohl daß es ein Tüchleindeckdich war.
sentences.l: “Now I notice,” said he, “in which kitchen there is cooking done for me; you shall be dearer to me than the mountain of silver and gold,” for he saw well that it was a little-cloth-cover-yourself.
sentences.i: “Now I see,” he said, “in what kitchen my meals are cooked. You shall be dearer to me than the mountain of silver and gold” — for he saw well that this was a cloth-lay-yourself.
sentences.n: Tüchleindeckdich is a name built straight out of the command “Tüchlein, deck dich”; it is the cloth cousin of the self-laying table in KHM 36. “für mich gekocht wird” is an impersonal passive: there is cooking done for me.

sentences.t: Das Tüchlein war ihm aber doch nicht genug, um sich daheim zur Ruhe zu setzen, sondern er wollte lieber noch in der Welt herum wandern und weiter sein Glück versuchen.
sentences.l: The little-cloth was however not enough for him, to set himself to rest at home; rather he would sooner still wander about in the world and try his fortune further.
sentences.i: Yet the little cloth was not enough to make him settle down at home; he would sooner roam the world a while yet and try his fortune further.
sentences.n: “sich zur Ruhe setzen” is the fixed phrase for settling down for good. “sein Glück versuchen” = to try one’s luck.

sentences.t: Eines Abends traf er in einem einsamen Walde einen schwarz bestaubten Köhler, der brannte da Kohlen, und hatte Kartoffeln am Feuer stehen, damit wollte er seine Mahlzeit halten.
sentences.l: One evening met he in a lonely forest a black-dusted charcoal-burner, who was burning charcoal there, and had potatoes standing at the fire, with which he wanted to hold his meal.
sentences.i: One evening, in a lonely forest, he met a charcoal-burner black with dust, who was burning charcoal there and had potatoes standing at the fire, meaning to make his meal of them.
sentences.n: A Köhler charred wood into charcoal out in the forest, camped for weeks beside his smouldering kiln — a proverbially poor and sooty trade. German says the potatoes stehen (stand) at the fire where English says they were on it.

sentences.t: „Guten Abend, du Schwarzamsel,“ sagte er, „wie geht dirs in deiner Einsamkeit?“
sentences.l: “Good evening, you black-ousel,” said he, “how goes it for you in your solitude?”
sentences.i: “Good evening, you black ousel,” he said, “how does it go with you in your solitude?”
sentences.n: Schwarzamsel — “black blackbird,” a teasing nickname for a man covered in soot. dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: „Einen Tag wie den andern,“ erwiederte der Köhler, „und jeden Abend Kartoffeln; hast du Lust dazu und willst mein Gast sein?“
sentences.l: “One day like the other,” answered the charcoal-burner, “and every evening potatoes; have you a mind for that and will you be my guest?”
sentences.i: “One day like the next,” answered the charcoal-burner, “and potatoes every evening. If you have a taste for them, will you be my guest?”
sentences.n: “Lust zu etwas haben” = to have a mind, an appetite for something. erwiederte is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte.

sentences.t: „Schönen Dank,“ antwortete der Reisende, „ich will dir die Mahlzeit nicht wegnehmen, du hast auf einen Gast nicht gerechnet, aber wenn du mit mir vorlieb nehmen willst, so sollst du eingeladen sein.“
sentences.l: “Fine thanks,” answered the traveler, “I will not take the meal away from you, you have not reckoned on a guest, but if you will make do with me, so you shall be invited.”
sentences.i: “My thanks,” answered the traveller, “I will not take your meal from you — you were not reckoning on a guest; but if you will take me as I come, then you shall be my guest instead.”
sentences.n: “vorlieb nehmen mit” = to be content with, to put up with what is offered.

sentences.t: „Wer soll dir anrichten?“ sprach der Köhler, „ich sehe daß du nichts bei dir hast, und ein paar Stunden im Umkreis ist niemand, der dir etwas geben könnte.“
sentences.l: “Who is to serve up for you?” spoke the charcoal-burner, “I see that you have nothing with you, and a couple of hours round about there is nobody who could give you anything.”
sentences.i: “And who is to dish up for you?” said the charcoal-burner. “I see you have nothing on you, and for a couple of hours around there is nobody who could give you a thing.”
sentences.n: anrichten is to prepare and set out food. Distance is reckoned in walking hours, the ordinary country measure.

sentences.t: „Und doch solls ein Essen sein,“ antwortete er, „so gut, wie du noch keins gekostet hast.“
sentences.l: “And yet it shall be a meal,” answered he, “so good as you have yet tasted none.”
sentences.i: “And yet there shall be a meal,” he answered, “such as you have never yet tasted.”
sentences.n: solls = soll es.

sentences.t: Darauf holte er sein Tüchlein aus dem Ranzen, breitete es auf die Erde, und sprach „Tüchlein, deck dich,“ und alsbald stand da Gesottenes und Gebratenes, und war so warm als wenn es eben aus der Küche käme.
sentences.l: Thereupon fetched he his little-cloth out of the knapsack, spread it on the earth, and spoke “little cloth, cover yourself,” and at once there stood boiled and roasted, and it was as warm as if it came just out of the kitchen.
sentences.i: Then he took his little cloth out of his knapsack, spread it on the ground, and said, “Little cloth, lay yourself” — and at once there stood boiled meats and roast, as warm as if it had come straight from the kitchen.
sentences.n: Gesottenes und Gebratenes are participles used as nouns, “boiled things and roasted things”: the standing pair for a full dinner. The Ranzen named here is still his own ordinary pack — the wonder-working knapsack of the title comes later, from this same charcoal-burner. käme is subjunctive after “als wenn.”

sentences.t: Der Köhler machte große Augen, ließ sich aber nicht lange bitten, sondern langte zu und schob immer größere Bissen in sein schwarzes Maul hinein.
sentences.l: The charcoal-burner made big eyes, let himself however not long be asked, but reached to and shoved ever bigger bites into his black maw.
sentences.i: The charcoal-burner’s eyes went wide; but he did not wait to be pressed — he fell to, and shoved bigger and bigger mouthfuls into his black jaws.
sentences.n: “große Augen machen” = to stare in astonishment; “sich nicht lange bitten lassen” = to need no second invitation; zulangen is to help oneself at table. Maul is an animal’s mouth, and coarse when used of a man.

sentences.t: Als sie abgegessen hatten, schmunzelte der Köhler und sagte „hör, dein Tüchlein hat meinen Beifall, das wäre so etwas für mich in dem Walde, wo mir niemand etwas gutes kocht.
sentences.l: When they had eaten up, the charcoal-burner smirked and said “listen, your little-cloth has my approval, that would be just something for me in the forest, where nobody cooks me anything good.
sentences.i: When they had eaten their fill, the charcoal-burner grinned and said: “Listen — that cloth of yours has my approval. It would be just the thing for me here in the forest, where nobody cooks me anything good.
sentences.n: schmunzeln is to smile with quiet, self-satisfied pleasure — the smile of a man who has just thought of something.

sentences.t: Ich will dir einen Tausch vorschlagen, da in der Ecke hängt ein Soldatenranzen, der zwar alt und unscheinbar ist, in dem aber wunderbare Kräfte stecken; da ich ihn doch nicht mehr brauche, so will ich ihn für das Tüchlein geben.“
sentences.l: I will propose you a trade: there in the corner hangs a soldier’s-knapsack, which is old and unremarkable indeed, but in which wonderful powers are lodged; since I have no more use for it, so I will give it for the little-cloth.”
sentences.i: I will propose a trade. There in the corner hangs a soldier’s knapsack — old and plain enough to look at, but wonderful powers are lodged in it; and since I have no more use for it, I will give it for the cloth.”
sentences.n: stecken is “to be stuck in,” hence to reside, to lie hidden in a thing. Two senses of da in one sentence: “there in the corner,” then “since, because.”

sentences.t: „Erst muß ich wissen was das für wunderbare Kräfte sind,“ erwiederte er.
sentences.l: “First must I know what sort of wonderful powers those are,” answered he.
sentences.i: “First I must know what sort of wonderful powers they are,” he replied.
sentences.n: “was für” = what sort of; the für governs nothing here.

sentences.t: „Das will ich dir sagen,“ antwortete der Köhler, „wenn du mit der Hand darauf klopfst, so kommt jedesmal ein Gefreiter mit sechs Mann, die haben Ober- und Untergewehr, und was du befiehlst, das vollbringen sie.“
sentences.l: “That will I tell you,” answered the charcoal-burner, “if you knock on it with the hand, so there comes each time a corporal with six man, they have upper- and under-weapon, and what you command, that they accomplish.”
sentences.i: “That I will tell you,” answered the charcoal-burner. “If you knock on it with your hand, each time a corporal comes with six men; they carry long-arm and side-arm, and whatever you command, they carry out.”
sentences.n: A Gefreiter is the lowest rank above a common soldier — a lance-corporal. “Ober- und Untergewehr” is old soldiers’ language for a man’s full arms: the firearm and the side-arm worn at the belt. German counts troops with Mann in the singular: “sechs Mann.”

sentences.t: „Meinetwegen,“ sagte er „wenns nicht anders sein kann, so wollen wir tauschen,“ gab dem Köhler das Tüchlein, hob den Ranzen von dem Haken, hieng ihn um und nahm Abschied.
sentences.l: “For my part,” said he, “if it cannot be otherwise, so we will trade,” gave the charcoal-burner the little-cloth, lifted the knapsack from the hook, hung it about him and took leave.
sentences.i: “Very well,” he said, “if it cannot be otherwise, then let us trade” — and he gave the charcoal-burner the cloth, lifted the knapsack off its hook, slung it over his shoulder and took his leave.
sentences.n: meinetwegen = “as far as I am concerned, all right then.” hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing, here from umhängen (to sling about oneself).

sentences.t: Als er ein Stück Wegs gegangen war, wollte er die Wunderkräfte seines Ranzens versuchen und klopfte darauf.
sentences.l: When he had gone a stretch of way, he wanted to try the wonder-powers of his knapsack and knocked on it.
sentences.i: When he had gone a stretch of the way he wanted to try out the wonder-powers of his knapsack, and knocked on it.

sentences.t: Alsbald traten die sieben Kriegshelden vor ihn, und der Gefreite sprach „was verlangt mein Herr und Gebieter?“
sentences.l: At once stepped the seven war-heroes before him, and the corporal spoke “what does my lord and commander demand?”
sentences.i: At once the seven warriors stepped before him, and the corporal said: “What does my lord and master require?”
sentences.n: Kriegshelden — “war-heroes” — is grandly said of seven conjured soldiers; the tale keeps a straight face. “Herr und Gebieter” is the formula addressed to the owner of a magic thing.

sentences.t: „Marschiert im Eilschritt zu dem Köhler und fordert mein Wünschtüchlein zurück.“
sentences.l: “March at the hurry-step to the charcoal-burner and demand my wish-cloth back.”
sentences.i: “March at the double to the charcoal-burner and demand my wishing-cloth back.”
sentences.n: Eilschritt is the military quick march. The imperatives are plural, addressed to the whole squad.

sentences.t: Sie machten links um, und gar nicht lange, so brachten sie das Verlangte und hatten es dem Köhler, ohne viel zu fragen, abgenommen.
sentences.l: They made left-about, and not long at all, so they brought the demanded thing and had taken it from the charcoal-burner without much asking.
sentences.i: They made a left turn, and it was no time at all before they brought what he had demanded — they had taken it from the charcoal-burner without much asking.
sentences.n: “links um” is the parade-ground command for a left turn. “das Verlangte” is a participle used as a noun: the thing demanded. The tale does not pretend this is anything but robbery, and spends no word on it.

sentences.t: Er hieß sie wieder abziehen, gieng weiter und hoffte das Glück würde ihm noch heller scheinen.
sentences.l: He bade them march off again, went further and hoped fortune would shine on him still more brightly.
sentences.i: He bade them march off again, went on his way, and hoped that fortune would shine on him brighter still.
sentences.n: heißen with a bare infinitive = to bid someone do something.

sentences.t: Bei Sonnenuntergang kam er zu einem andern Köhler, der bei dem Feuer seine Abendmahlzeit bereitete.
sentences.l: At sundown came he to another charcoal-burner, who was preparing his evening meal by the fire.
sentences.i: At sundown he came to another charcoal-burner, who was preparing his evening meal by the fire.

sentences.t: „Willst du mit mir essen,“ sagte der rußige Geselle, „Kartoffeln mit Salz aber ohne Schmalz, so setz dich zu mir nieder.“
sentences.l: “Will you eat with me,” said the sooty fellow, “potatoes with salt but without lard, then sit yourself down beside me.”
sentences.i: “If you will eat with me,” said the sooty fellow — “potatoes with salt but no dripping — then sit down here beside me.”
sentences.n: “mit Salz aber ohne Schmalz” rhymes in the German: the barest fare there is. Schmalz is rendered pork fat, the poor man’s butter.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete er, „für diesmal sollst du mein Gast sein,“ deckte sein Tüchlein auf, das gleich mit den schönsten Gerichten besetzt war.
sentences.l: “No,” answered he, “for this time you shall be my guest,” laid his little-cloth out, which was at once set with the finest dishes.
sentences.i: “No,” he answered, “this time you shall be my guest” — and he laid his cloth out, and it was set at once with the finest dishes.
sentences.n: aufdecken here is to lay a cloth or a table out for a meal, not to uncover something.

sentences.t: Sie aßen und tranken zusammen und waren guter Dinge.
sentences.l: They ate and drank together and were of good things.
sentences.i: They ate and drank together and were in good spirits.
sentences.n: “guter Dinge sein” is a genitive idiom: to be in good spirits, merry.

sentences.t: Nach dem Essen sprach der Kohlenbrenner „da oben auf der Kammbank liegt ein altes abgegriffenes Hütlein, das hat seltsame Eigenschaften: wenn das einer aufsetzt und dreht es auf dem Kopf herum, so gehen die Feldschlangen, als wären zwölfe neben einander aufgeführt, und schießen alles darnieder, daß niemand dagegen bestehen kann.
sentences.l: After the meal spoke the coal-burner “up there on the shelf lies an old worn little-hat, that has strange properties: if someone puts it on and turns it about on the head, so the field-serpents go off as though twelve were drawn up side by side, and shoot everything down, so that nobody can stand against it.
sentences.i: After the meal the charcoal-burner said: “Up there on the shelf lies an old worn little hat, and it has strange properties: if a man puts it on and turns it round on his head, the field-guns go off as though twelve of them were drawn up side by side, and shoot everything down, so that nobody can stand against them.
sentences.n: A Feldschlange — “field serpent” — is an old long-barrelled field cannon, the culverin, named for its slender shape. Kammbank is a rare word: some kind of shelf or ledge in the hut, though the exact fitting is uncertain. zwölfe is an old inflected form of zwölf.

sentences.t: Mir nützt das Hütlein nichts und für dein Tischtuch will ichs wohl hingeben.“
sentences.l: To me the little-hat is of no use and for your tablecloth I will readily give it away.”
sentences.i: The little hat is no use to me, and for your tablecloth I will gladly part with it.”
sentences.n: ichs = ich es; hingeben is to hand over, give away.

sentences.t: „Das läßt sich hören,“ antwortete er, nahm das Hütlein, setzte es auf und ließ sein Tüchlein zurück.
sentences.l: “That lets itself be heard,” answered he, took the little-hat, set it on and left his little-cloth behind.
sentences.i: “That is worth hearing,” he answered; and he took the little hat, put it on, and left his cloth behind.
sentences.n: “das läßt sich hören” is a set phrase: that is an offer worth listening to.

sentences.t: Kaum aber war er ein Stück Wegs gegangen, so klopfte er auf seinen Ranzen, und seine Soldaten mußten ihm das Tüchlein wieder holen.
sentences.l: But scarcely had he gone a stretch of way, so he knocked on his knapsack, and his soldiers had to fetch him the little-cloth back.
sentences.i: But scarcely had he gone a stretch of the way when he knocked on his knapsack, and his soldiers had to fetch the cloth back for him.

sentences.t: „Es kommt eins zum andern,“ dachte er, „und es ist mir, als wäre mein Glück noch nicht zu Ende.“
sentences.l: “One thing comes to the other,” thought he, “and it is to me as if my fortune were not yet at an end.”
sentences.i: “One thing comes upon another,” he thought, “and it seems to me my fortune is not yet at an end.”
sentences.n: “es ist mir, als…” = it seems to me as if, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Seine Gedanken hatten ihn auch nicht betrogen.
sentences.l: His thoughts had indeed not deceived him.
sentences.i: Nor had his thoughts deceived him.
sentences.n: auch here is not “also” but a confirming particle: sure enough, and so it proved.

sentences.t: Nachdem er abermals einen Tag gegangen war, kam er zu einem dritten Köhler, der ihn nicht anders als die vorigen zu ungeschmelzten Kartoffeln einlud.
sentences.l: After he had gone another day, came he to a third charcoal-burner, who invited him, no differently than the previous ones, to unlarded potatoes.
sentences.i: After walking another day he came to a third charcoal-burner, who invited him, just as the others had, to potatoes without dripping.
sentences.n: ungeschmelzt — with no melted fat poured over them; the third charcoal-burner is as poor as the other two.

sentences.t: Er ließ ihn aber von seinem Wunschtüchlein mitessen, und das schmeckte dem Köhler so gut, daß er ihm zuletzt ein Hörnlein dafür bot, das noch ganz andere Eigenschaften hatte als das Hütlein.
sentences.l: He let him however eat along from his wish-cloth, and that tasted so good to the charcoal-burner that at last he offered him a little-horn for it, which had quite other properties still than the little-hat.
sentences.i: But he let the man eat with him from his wishing-cloth, and it tasted so good to the charcoal-burner that in the end he offered him a little horn for it — one with properties of quite another order than the hat’s.
sentences.n: German makes the food the subject: “das schmeckte dem Köhler” — it tasted good to him.

sentences.t: Wenn man darauf blies, so fielen alle Mauern und Festungswerke, endlich alle Städte und Dörfer übern Haufen.
sentences.l: If one blew on it, so all walls and fortification-works fell, at last all towns and villages, over the heap.
sentences.i: If a man blew on it, all walls and fortifications fell in ruin, and at last all towns and villages too.
sentences.n: “über den Haufen fallen” = to collapse in a heap; übern is the spoken contraction of über den.

sentences.t: Er gab dem Köhler zwar das Tüchlein dafür, ließ sichs aber hernach von seiner Mannschaft wieder abfordern, so daß er endlich Ranzen, Hütlein und Hörnlein beisammen hatte.
sentences.l: He gave the charcoal-burner the little-cloth for it indeed, but had it demanded back for himself afterward by his troop, so that at last he had knapsack, little-hat and little-horn together.
sentences.i: He did give the charcoal-burner the cloth for it, but afterwards had his troop demand it back for him, so that at last he had knapsack, hat and horn all together.
sentences.n: “ließ sichs abfordern” is causative: he had it demanded back for himself; sichs = sich es.

sentences.t: „Jetzt,“ sprach er, „bin ich ein gemachter Mann, und es ist Zeit, daß ich heimkehre und sehe wie es meinen Brüdern ergeht.“
sentences.l: “Now,” spoke he, “am I a made man, and it is time that I turn homeward and see how it goes for my brothers.”
sentences.i: “Now,” he said, “I am a made man; and it is time I turned homeward and saw how my brothers are faring.”
sentences.n: “wie es einem ergeht” = how someone is faring, with the impersonal es and the person in the dative.

sentences.t: Als er daheim anlangte, hatten sich seine Brüder von ihrem Silber und Gold ein schönes Haus gebaut und lebten in Saus und Braus.
sentences.l: When he arrived at home, his brothers had built themselves a fine house from their silver and gold and lived in rush and roar.
sentences.i: When he arrived home, his brothers had built themselves a fine house out of their silver and gold, and were living high.
sentences.n: “in Saus und Braus leben” = to live it up in noisy luxury — Saus a rushing, Braus a roaring; neither word survives outside the pair.

sentences.t: Er trat bei ihnen ein, weil er aber in einem halb zerrissenen Rock kam, das schäbige Hütlein auf dem Kopf und den alten Ranzen auf dem Rücken, so wollten sie ihn nicht für ihren Bruder anerkennen.
sentences.l: He stepped in with them, but because he came in a half-torn coat, the shabby little-hat on the head and the old knapsack on the back, so they would not acknowledge him for their brother.
sentences.i: He stepped in to them; but because he came in a half-tattered coat, the shabby little hat on his head and the old knapsack on his back, they would not own him for their brother.
sentences.n: Rock here is a man’s coat, its older sense.

sentences.t: Sie spotteten und sagten „du gibst dich für unsern Bruder aus, der Silber und Gold verschmähte, und für sich ein besseres Glück verlangte: der kommt gewiß in voller Pracht als ein mächtiger König angefahren, nicht als ein Bettelmann,“ und jagten ihn zur Thüre hinaus.
sentences.l: They mocked and said “you give yourself out for our brother, who scorned silver and gold and demanded a better fortune for himself: that one comes surely driving up in full splendour as a mighty king, not as a beggar-man,” and chased him out the door.
sentences.i: They mocked him and said: “You give yourself out for our brother — he who scorned silver and gold and demanded a better fortune for himself? He will come driving up in full splendour as a mighty king, not as a beggarman.” And they drove him out of doors.
sentences.n: “sich ausgeben für” = to pass oneself off as. “kommt angefahren” uses a participle after kommen for the manner of arriving, as with kam gekrochen elsewhere in these tales.

sentences.t: Da gerieth er in Zorn, klopfte auf seinen Ranzen so lange bis hundert und funfzig Mann in Reih und Glied vor ihm standen.
sentences.l: Then fell he into anger, knocked on his knapsack so long until a hundred and fifty men stood before him in rank and file.
sentences.i: At that he flew into a rage, and knocked on his knapsack until a hundred and fifty men stood before him in rank and file.
sentences.n: funfzig is the 1857 spelling of fünfzig. “in Reih und Glied” is the drill formation: rank and file.

sentences.t: Er befahl ihnen das Haus seiner Brüder zu umzingeln, und zwei sollten Haselgerten mitnehmen und den beiden übermüthigen die Haut auf dem Leib so lange weich gerben, bis sie wüßten wer er wäre.
sentences.l: He commanded them to surround the house of his brothers, and two were to take hazel-switches along and to tan the skin on the body of the two arrogant ones soft, until they knew who he was.
sentences.i: He ordered them to surround his brothers’ house, and two were to bring hazel switches and tan the hides of the two overweening brothers until they knew who he was.
sentences.n: “die Haut weich gerben” — literally to tan the skin soft: the tanner’s trade turned into a beating. Hazel switches were the standard rod. wüßten and wäre are subjunctive inside the order.

sentences.t: Es entstand ein gewaltiger Lärm, die Leute liefen zusammen und wollten den beiden in der Noth Beistand leisten, aber sie konnten gegen die Soldaten nichts ausrichten.
sentences.l: There arose a mighty uproar, the people ran together and wanted to render the two assistance in their need, but they could accomplish nothing against the soldiers.
sentences.i: A mighty uproar arose; people came running together and meant to stand by the two in their distress, but they could do nothing against the soldiers.
sentences.n: “Beistand leisten” = to render assistance. “nichts ausrichten” — to get nowhere, achieve nothing — recurs three times in this stretch of the tale.

sentences.t: Es geschah endlich dem Könige Meldung davon der ward unwillig, und ließ einen Hauptmann mit seiner Schaar ausrücken, der sollte den Ruhestörer aus der Stadt jagen: aber der Mann mit dem Ranzen hatte bald eine größere Mannschaft zusammen, die schlug den Hauptmann mit seinen Leuten zurück, daß sie mit blutigen Nasen abziehen mußten.
sentences.l: At last there happened report of it to the king; he became displeased, and had a captain march out with his troop, who was to chase the peace-disturber out of the city: but the man with the knapsack soon had a greater force together, which beat the captain with his people back, so that they had to withdraw with bloody noses.
sentences.i: At last report of it reached the king, and he was displeased, and sent a captain marching out with his company to drive the disturber of the peace out of the city; but the man with the knapsack soon had a larger force together, and it beat the captain and his men back, so that they had to withdraw with bloody noses.
sentences.n: “es geschah dem Könige Meldung davon” is old officialese: report of it was made to the king. The 1857 text runs straight on into “davon der ward unwillig” without punctuation — we keep it. Schaar = modern Schar, a troop or band.

sentences.t: Der König sprach „der hergelaufene Kerl ist noch zu bändigen,“ und schickte am andern Tage eine größere Schaar gegen ihn aus, aber sie konnte noch weniger ausrichten.
sentences.l: The king spoke “the fellow come running from nowhere is still to be tamed,” and sent out the next day a greater troop against him, but it could accomplish still less.
sentences.i: The king said: “That vagabond fellow can still be brought to heel,” and next day sent out a larger troop against him; but it achieved even less.
sentences.n: hergelaufen — “come running from somewhere” — is said contemptuously of a rootless nobody. “ist zu bändigen”: sein + zu + infinitive states possibility, “can be tamed.”

sentences.t: Er stellte noch mehr Volk entgegen, und um noch schneller fertig zu werden, drehte er ein paarmal sein Hütlein auf dem Kopfe herum: da fieng das schwere Geschütz an zu spielen, und des Königs Leute wurden geschlagen und in die Flucht gejagt.
sentences.l: He set still more folk against them, and in order to be finished still faster, he turned his little-hat a couple of times about on the head: then began the heavy artillery to play, and the king’s people were beaten and chased into flight.
sentences.i: He set still more men against them; and to be done the sooner, he turned his little hat a couple of times round on his head — whereupon the heavy guns began to play, and the king’s men were beaten and put to flight.
sentences.n: German has guns “play” (spielen), the same metaphor behind English “to play upon” a target.

sentences.t: „Jetzt mache ich nicht eher Frieden,“ sprach er, „als bis mir der König seine Tochter zur Frau gibt, und ich in seinem Namen das ganze Reich beherrsche.“
sentences.l: “Now make I no peace sooner,” spoke he, “than until the king gives me his daughter to wife, and I rule the whole realm in his name.”
sentences.i: “Now I will make no peace,” he said, “until the king gives me his daughter to wife and I rule the whole realm in his name.”
sentences.n: “nicht eher… als bis” = not until; the two halves belong together across the speech tag. “zur Frau geben” is the formula for giving in marriage.

sentences.t: Das ließ er dem König verkündigen, und dieser sprach zu seiner Tochter „Muß ist eine harte Nuß: was bleibt mir anders übrig, als daß ich thue was er verlangt? will ich Frieden haben und die Krone auf meinem Haupte behalten, so muß ich dich hingeben.“
sentences.l: That let he be proclaimed to the king, and this one spoke to his daughter “Must is a hard nut: what else remains over to me than that I do what he demands? will I have peace and keep the crown on my head, so must I give you away.”
sentences.i: This he had proclaimed to the king, and the king said to his daughter: “‘Must’ is a hard nut. What else is left me but to do what he demands? If I am to have peace and keep the crown on my head, I must give you up.”
sentences.n: “Muß ist eine harte Nuß” is a proverb: necessity is a hard nut to crack. A conditional clause can drop wenn and lead with the verb instead — “will ich Frieden haben” = if I want peace.

sentences.t: Die Hochzeit ward also gefeiert, aber die Königstochter war verdrießlich daß ihr Gemahl ein gemeiner Mann war, der einen schäbigen Hut trug und einen alten Ranzen umhängen hatte.
sentences.l: The wedding was thus celebrated, but the king’s-daughter was vexed that her husband was a common man, who wore a shabby hat and had an old knapsack slung about him.
sentences.i: So the wedding was celebrated; but the king’s daughter was sullen that her husband was a common man who wore a shabby hat and had an old knapsack slung over his shoulder.
sentences.n: gemein keeps its older sense here — common, of low birth — not “mean.”

sentences.t: Sie wäre ihn gerne wieder los gewesen und sann Tag und Nacht wie sie das bewerkstelligen könnte.
sentences.l: She would gladly have been rid of him again and pondered day and night how she might bring that about.
sentences.n: “jemanden los sein” = to be rid of someone. sinnen (sann) is to brood on a thing, to turn it over.

sentences.t: Da dachte sie „sollten seine Wunderkräfte wohl in dem Ranzen stecken?“ verstellte sich und liebkoste ihm, und als sein Herz weich geworden war, sprach sie „wenn du nur den schlechten Ranzen ablegen wolltest, er verunziert dich so sehr, daß ich mich deiner schämen muß.“
sentences.l: Then thought she “should his wonder-powers be lodged in the knapsack?” dissembled herself and caressed him, and when his heart had grown soft, spoke she “if you would only lay the wretched knapsack aside, it disfigures you so much that I must be ashamed of you.”
sentences.i: Then she thought: “Could his wonder-powers be lodged in the knapsack?” She dissembled and made much of him; and when his heart had grown soft she said: “If only you would put that wretched knapsack aside — it disfigures you so that I must be ashamed of you.”
sentences.n: sollten… wohl marks a guess: might they be…? “sich schämen” takes the genitive — “ich schäme mich deiner,” I am ashamed of you. liebkosen with the dative (ihm) is old usage; modern German takes the accusative.

sentences.t: „Liebes Kind,“ antwortete er, „dieser Ranzen ist mein größter Schatz, so lange ich den habe, fürchte ich keine Macht der Welt;“ und verrieth ihr mit welchen Wunderkräften er begabt war.
sentences.l: “Dear child,” answered he, “this knapsack is my greatest treasure, so long as I have it, I fear no power of the world;” and betrayed to her with what wonder-powers it was endowed.
sentences.i: “Dear child,” he answered, “this knapsack is my greatest treasure; as long as I have it I fear no power on earth” — and he betrayed to her what wonder-powers it was endowed with.
sentences.n: In “mit welchen Wunderkräften er begabt war,” er is the Ranzen (a masculine noun), so “what powers it was endowed with” — though the German would also bear “he,” meaning the man himself. verrieth = modern verriet.

sentences.t: Da fiel sie ihm um den Hals, als wenn sie ihn küssen wollte, nahm ihm aber mit Behendigkeit den Ranzen von der Schulter und lief damit fort.
sentences.l: Then fell she to him about the neck, as if she wanted to kiss him, but took the knapsack from his shoulder with nimbleness and ran away with it.
sentences.i: Then she fell on his neck as if she meant to kiss him, but deftly lifted the knapsack from his shoulder and ran off with it.
sentences.n: “jemandem um den Hals fallen” = to throw one’s arms round someone, the person standing in the dative.

sentences.t: Sobald sie allein war, klopfte sie darauf und befahl den Kriegsleuten sie sollten ihren vorigen Herrn festnehmen und aus dem königlichen Palast fortführen.
sentences.l: As soon as she was alone, she knocked on it and commanded the war-men they should seize their previous master and lead him away out of the royal palace.
sentences.i: As soon as she was alone she knocked on it and ordered the soldiers to seize their former master and carry him out of the royal palace.

sentences.t: Sie gehorchten, und die falsche Frau ließ noch mehr Leute hinter ihm her ziehen, die ihn ganz zum Lande hinaus jagen sollten.
sentences.l: They obeyed, and the false woman had still more people draw along behind him, who were to chase him quite out of the country.
sentences.i: They obeyed; and the false woman had yet more men march after him, to chase him clean out of the country.
sentences.n: falsch here is treacherous, false-hearted, not “incorrect.”

sentences.t: Da wäre er verloren gewesen, wenn er nicht das Hütlein gehabt hätte.
sentences.l: Then would he have been lost, if he had not had the little-hat.
sentences.i: He would have been lost then, had he not had the little hat.
sentences.n: The unreal past in both halves: wäre … gewesen and hätte … gehabt, both subjunctive II — what would have happened and did not.

sentences.t: Kaum aber waren seine Hände frei, so schwenkte er es ein paar mal: alsbald fieng das Geschütz an zu donnern und schlug alles nieder, und die Königstochter mußte selbst kommen und um Gnade bitten.
sentences.l: But scarcely were his hands free, so he swung it a couple of times: at once began the artillery to thunder and struck everything down, and the king’s-daughter had to come herself and beg for mercy.
sentences.i: But scarcely were his hands free when he swung it round a couple of times — at once the guns began to thunder and struck everything down, and the king’s daughter had to come herself and beg for mercy.
sentences.n: This time he only swings the hat rather than turning it on his head; the tale is not strict about its own rules.

sentences.t: Weil sie so beweglich bat und sich zu bessern versprach, so ließ er sich überreden und bewilligte ihr Frieden.
sentences.l: Because she pleaded so movingly and promised to better herself, so he let himself be persuaded and granted her peace.
sentences.i: Because she pleaded so movingly and promised to mend her ways, he let himself be persuaded and granted her peace.
sentences.n: beweglich here has its older active sense — moving, affecting — not “movable.”

sentences.t: Sie that freundlich mit ihm, stellte sich an als hätte sie ihn sehr lieb und wußte ihn nach einiger Zeit so zu bethören daß er ihr vertraute wenn auch einer den Ranzen in seine Gewalt bekäme, so könnte er doch nichts gegen ihn ausrichten so lange das alte Hütlein noch sein wäre.
sentences.l: She did friendly with him, made as though she loved him very much, and after some time knew so to befool him that he confided to her, even if someone got the knapsack into his power, he could still accomplish nothing against him so long as the old little-hat were his.
sentences.i: She behaved kindly toward him, put on an act as though she loved him dearly, and after a time knew how to befool him so far that he confided to her that even if someone got the knapsack into his power, he could still do nothing against him so long as the old hat was his.
sentences.n: “freundlich thun mit jemandem” = to behave affectionately toward someone; “sich anstellen als” = to put on an act; bethören = modern betören, to beguile. The whole confidence stands in the subjunctive (bekäme, könnte, wäre): his words, not the narrator’s fact.

sentences.t: Als sie das Geheimnis wußte, wartete sie bis er eingeschlafen war, dann nahm sie ihm das Hütlein weg, und ließ ihn hinaus auf die Straße werfen.
sentences.l: When she knew the secret, she waited until he had fallen asleep, then took she the little-hat away from him, and had him thrown out into the street.
sentences.i: When she knew the secret she waited until he had fallen asleep; then she took the hat away from him and had him thrown out into the street.

sentences.t: Aber noch war ihm das Hörnlein übrig, und in großem Zorne blies er aus allen Kräften hinein.
sentences.l: But the little-horn was still left to him, and in great anger he blew into it with all his forces.
sentences.i: But the little horn was still left him, and in great anger he blew into it with all his might.

sentences.t: Alsbald fiel alles zusammen, Mauern, Festungswerk, Städte und Dörfer, und schlugen den König und die Königstochter todt.
sentences.l: At once fell everything together, walls, fortification-work, towns and villages, and struck the king and the king’s-daughter dead.
sentences.i: At once everything collapsed — walls, fortifications, towns and villages — and struck the king and the king’s daughter dead.
sentences.n: The verb schlugen is plural, agreeing with the listed things rather than with alles. todt = modern tot.

sentences.t: Und wenn er das Hörnlein nicht abgesetzt und nur noch ein wenig länger geblasen hätte, so wäre alles über den Haufen gestürzt und kein Stein auf dem andern geblieben.
sentences.l: And if he had not set the little-horn down and had blown only a little longer, so would everything have been thrown over the heap and no stone have remained upon the other.
sentences.i: And if he had not taken the horn from his lips, but had blown a little longer, everything would have been thrown down in ruins and no stone left upon another.
sentences.n: absetzen here is to take the instrument from one’s mouth. “kein Stein auf dem andern” has a biblical ring: the phrase for total destruction.

sentences.t: Da widerstand ihm niemand mehr, und er setzte sich zum König über das ganze Reich.
sentences.l: Then withstood him nobody any more, and he set himself as king over the whole realm.
sentences.i: After that nobody withstood him any more, and he set himself up as king over the whole realm.
sentences.n: The tale ends with no blessing and no formula — the third brother simply keeps what force has won him.
